props.title: The Video Dead

sections.content: The Video Dead stands as a deliciously bizarre entry in the "killer technology" horror subgenre that exploded in the 1980s. While Poltergeist (1982) used the TV as a portal to supernatural terror, and Videodrome (1983) explored body horror through broadcast signals, The Video Dead takes a gleefully low-budget approach: zombies simply crawl out of a cursed television set to terrorize suburbia. The film's DIY practical effects and intentionally campy tone make it a perfect example of the direct-to-video horror boom that defined late 80s genre filmmaking.

sections.content: The late 1980s saw an explosion of horror films dealing with consumer technology gone wrong. Pulse (1988) turned household electricity murderous, while Remote Control (1988) featured mind-controlling VHS tapes. This trend reflected growing anxieties about technology's increasing presence in American homes. The Video Dead taps directly into fears about television's hypnotic power over viewers - literally making them braindead through endless consumption.

Director Robert Scott's only feature film deserves recognition for its creative zombie makeup effects achieved on a microscopic budget. While contemporary films like Day of the Dead (1985) had millions to work with, The Video Dead created memorable undead on pocket change. The zombies' design - with their exaggerated grins and eerily casual behavior - influenced later meta-horror films like Idle Hands (1999). SUBHEAD: Television Horror Evolution

sections.content: The Video Dead's influence can be traced through later technology-based horror films. Ringu (1998) and its American remake The Ring (2002) adopted similar concepts of cursed media, while movies like White Noise (2005) and FeardotCom (2002) continued exploring electronic devices as conduits for supernatural evil. Even modern films like Host (2020) carry The Video Dead's DNA, replacing TV sets with Zoom calls as portals for horror.
